Deleterious

del-ih-TEER-ee-us -- from Greek dēlētērios ('noxious'), rooted in deleisthai ('to hurt, injure'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Deleterious is causing harm or damage, especially in a gradual or not-immediately-obvious way.

The nutritionist explained that a diet heavy in processed sugar could have a deleterious effect on a growing child's energy levels.

Worked Example

Years of construction dust turned out to have a deleterious effect on the workers' lung health, even though none of them felt sick at first.

The harm builds up slowly and isn't obvious right away -- exactly the kind of gradual, damaging effect deleterious describes.

How Deleterious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

harmful

harmful: causing or likely to cause damage

detrimental

detrimental: tending to cause harm

Antonyms

beneficial

beneficial: producing good or helpful results

salutary

salutary: having a good or wholesome effect

How Strong Is It? — harmful → detrimental → deleterious

harmful vs. deleterious

harmful vs. deleterious: Too much screen time before bed can be mildly harmful to a good night's sleep.

detrimental vs. deleterious

detrimental vs. deleterious: The layoffs proved detrimental to morale for the rest of the year.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Deleterious traces back to Greek deleisthai, 'to hurt or injure' -- a deleter was a destroyer. Unlike many Greek roots, this one never went on to build other common English words.

Use the root in a new word: deleterious effect

Use the root in a new word: deleterious effect: Deleterious almost always appears paired with the word effect or effects in formal writing -- 'a deleterious effect on the ecosystem' is far more common than deleterious used alone.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Deleterious is a formal, often scientific word -- it's most at home describing measurable harm to health, the environment, or a system, rather than everyday unpleasantness.
